newsitem.title: FRANCE: Elf has big rise in 1996 profits.
newsitem.headline: Elf has big rise in 1996 profits.

text.p: Elf-Aquitaine SA on Wednesday reported a big jump in 1996 net income, helped by a rise in oil prices and efficiency efforts.
The net income excluding special items rose to 7.518 billion francs ($1.3 billion) from 5.325 billion, on sales of 232.7 billion against 208.29 billion in 1995.
The dividend was raised to a net 14 francs cash per share, from 13 and earnings per share were up at 28 francs from 20 francs.

"This improvement is not only due to high oil prices. Our course would not have been as satisfying if we had not developed our businesses while continuing to reduce our costs," chairman Philippe Jaffre said in a statement.

"Our objective is to grow Elf's value for shareholders by transforming Elf from a European company into a leading international corporation with a level of profitability which is equal to the best," he added.
Chief financial officer Bruno Weymuller said that Elf's return on equity had increased to 9.5 percent from 6.9 percent in 1995, but that of the other oil majors was currently above 11 percent.
"We want to reduce that gap," he told reporters.
Elf did not make a forecast for 1997, saying this depended largely on the evolution in crude oil prices. It said crude's recent high levels were unlikely to be sustained.

"A relaxation of oil prices would be likely to have a favourable effect on refining and petrochemical margins, provided that the European, North American and Asian economies maintain a good level of activity," Elf said in a statement.
Weymuller added that a change of $1.0 in the price of Brent oil would have an impact in the same direction of 1.5 billion francs on the operating income of production and refining.
A rise of 0.50 francs in the dollar/franc exchange rate would also boost operating income at exploration and production by 1.5 billion francs.
But he said that oil prices were likely to fall and the dollar was currently relatively high.
He said he aimed to further internationalise Elf.
"Elf has raised itself to among the top 10 oil companies in the world, among the first 20 chemical groups of the world and among the 30 leading international pharmaceutical companies," he said.

"But today our markets, our activities are three-quarters European. The European Union, its internal market is (Elf's) main market. It is not yet a world company in the true sense of the word," Jaffre said.
"In 2005, Elf will be a world company with 40 percent of its activities in America, Asia and Africa. In all of its activities it will be among the top 10 in the respective sectors," he said.
In the year 2000, Elf already aims to generate a third of its sales outside Europe against a quarter now.
In the oil sector, Elf is already number eight in the world.
"Historically we always grew quicker than the average of our competitors. But for a number of years that was not the case. It will be the case again," Jaffre said.

The oil sector will increase its production and reserves, create a third group of production units on a east-west axis -- Latin America and Middle East -- on top of its north-south axis of the North Sea and the Gulf of Guinea.
It will also develop its natural gas activities and make its refining and distribution activities more profitable. Elf said its German distribution operations would be profitable in 1997.

In chemicals, the Elf Atochem division, the company is number 12 in the world. It aims to be low cost producer of basic chemicals and expand in specialty chemicals -- such as adhesives -- by acquisitions.
"Its strategic goal is to make two-thirds of its sales in specialty chemicals in 2000," Jaffre said.
This compares to half of the sales in 1996.

In health, Elf has a 55 percent stake in Sanofi which is number 23 on the world scale. Elf announced earlier this year that it was willing to cut back its stake in Sanofi if the latter found a suitable merger partner.
Jaffre explained on Wednesday that for Sanofi to get into the top 10, and with the current price-earnings ratios in the durgs sector, an acquisition was not possible.
But a merger, in which Elf would have a smaller participation in a bigger group, would be possible.

Sanofi chairman and Elf board member Jean-Francois Dehecq declined to be drawn into indicating directly whether he would want to expand into the U.S. or into Europe, adding the future merger depended on opportunities.

But he said that through an alliance with Bristol-Myers Squibb it had a sufficient sales force to sell its new products in North America and added that Sanofi needed to be strong in its European home market to be strong world-wide.
Jaffre said that the cost reduction at exploration and production had continued to $2.9 per barrel from $4.4 in 1993, while production had increased to more than one million barrels per day.

"In three years time the rhythm of growth will accelerate," Jaffre said, adding the company's reserves, at 3.302 million barrels -- against 3.364 million in 1995 -- represented nine years of production.
In 1996, the operating income at exploration and production was up to 15.494 billion francs from 8.008 billion in 1995, after 241 million in restructuring charges.
In refining, marketing and trading, operating income was up to 147 million francs from four million in 1995. The 1996 figure included 300 million francs in restructuring charges.
In chemicals, operating income fell to 3.645 billion francs from 4.959 billion francs.
In health, the operating income slipped to 2.458 billion francs fom 2.489 billion. ($ = 5.637 French Francs) (c) Reuters Limited 1997
